learning_objective: Understand the fundamental structural and execution differences between processes and threads, shared versus private thread resources, concurrency versus parallelism, thread states, thread scheduling, synchronization challenges like race conditions and deadlocks, and practical constructs like thread pools.
audience_level: Undergraduate Computer Science & Operating Systems Students
visual_strategy: Use a clear spatial box model for processes containing shared memory spaces (Code, Data, Heap) and localized execution pipelines for threads (Stack, Registers, PC). Use dynamic color-coded execution arrows, side-by-side split screens for single-core vs. multi-core processing, structured state machine nodes for lifecycle changes, and step-by-step timeline interactions to visually demonstrate race conditions and deadlock cycles.
key_concepts: Shared Resources vs. Private Thread Context

scenes.title: Process vs. Thread Anatomy
scenes.purpose: Demonstrate visually what memory is shared within a process and what is private to each thread.
scenes.narration: A process defines an isolated execution environment with shared resources. Threads reside inside the process, sharing code, data, and heap memory, but maintaining their own stack, registers, and program counter.

visual_objects.label: Process Address Space
visual_objects.purpose: Represents the boundary of the operating system process.

visual_objects.label: Code Section
visual_objects.purpose: Shows the memory region shared across all threads containing application code.

visual_objects.label: Data Section
visual_objects.purpose: Shows global and static memory shared by all threads.

visual_objects.label: Heap Space
visual_objects.purpose: Shows dynamically allocated memory available to every thread in the process.

visual_objects.label: Thread 1
visual_objects.purpose: Encapsulates private storage for the first thread.

visual_objects.label: PC & Registers
visual_objects.purpose: Shows thread 1 independent CPU execution pointers.

visual_objects.label: Thread 2
visual_objects.purpose: Encapsulates private storage for the second thread.

visual_objects.label: PC & Registers
visual_objects.purpose: Shows thread 2 independent execution pointers operating on different instructions.

relationships.importance: Demonstrates that Thread 1 can access common heap memory.
Demonstrates that Thread 2 accesses the exact same heap memory.

actions.description: Draw the main process bounding box.
actions.educational_reason: Establishes the boundary of the operating system process.

actions.description: Fade in shared Code section.
actions.educational_reason: Shows the shared code base available to all threads.

actions.description: Fade in shared Data section.
actions.educational_reason: Shows shared global state across threads.

actions.description: Fade in shared Heap section.
actions.educational_reason: Shows dynamic memory shared by all threads.

actions.description: Expand Thread 1 private context containing its unique stack and registers.
actions.educational_reason: Visually separates shared process memory from private thread state.

actions.description: Expand Thread 2 private context alongside Thread 1.
actions.educational_reason: Proves that multiple execution contexts can co-exist within one process.

actions.description: Highlight PC values of both threads simultaneously.
actions.educational_reason: Emphasizes that each thread executes its own program counter independently.

scenes.transition_to_next: Smoothly transition the execution paths into CPU hardware execution cores.

scenes.title: Concurrency vs. Parallelism
scenes.purpose: Visually differentiate time-sliced single-core execution (concurrency) from physical simultaneous multicore execution (parallelism).
scenes.narration: Concurrency means multiple tasks make progress during overlapping time intervals via rapid context switching. Parallelism means tasks execute literally at the exact same time on distinct physical CPU cores.

visual_objects.label: Single-Core CPU
visual_objects.purpose: Represents a single hardware execution core.

visual_objects.label: Active CPU Slot
visual_objects.purpose: Shows which thread currently holds the single core.

relationships.importance: Links time slicing concept to single core.
Highlights simultaneous activity on dual cores.

actions.description: Display single core processor box on left.
actions.educational_reason: Establishes single-core hardware constraint.

actions.description: Display quad-core processor box on right.
actions.educational_reason: Establishes multicore hardware capability.

actions.description: Rapidly switch single core label back and forth between 'Thread 1 (Orange)' and 'Thread 2 (Green)'.
actions.educational_reason: Visually demonstrates concurrency via rapid time-slicing on one processor.

actions.description: Show Core 1 actively running Thread 1 continuously.
actions.educational_reason: Shows persistent active running state on first core.

actions.description: Show Core 2 actively running Thread 2 at the exact same time instance.
actions.educational_reason: Proves true hardware parallelism.

scenes.transition_to_next: Transform single thread activity into a formal OS Lifecycle State Machine.

scenes.title: Thread Lifecycle and Context Switching
scenes.purpose: Show how threads transition between lifecycle states and how the Thread Control Block (TCB) preserves context during switching.
scenes.narration: The operating system manages threads using Thread Control Blocks. As threads shift between Ready, Running, and Blocked states, context switching saves the old thread execution state and restores the new thread state.

visual_objects.label: Blocked / Waiting
visual_objects.purpose: Waiting for I/O or lock release.

visual_objects.label: TCB (Thread Control Block)
visual_objects.content: TID: 101 | State: Running | PC: 0x4012 | Registers: Saved
visual_objects.purpose: Data structure maintaining OS context for thread preemption and restoration.

visual_objects.label: Thread A
visual_objects.purpose: Moving token representing the currently tracked thread.

actions.description: Display the TCB structure overhead.
actions.educational_reason: Introduces the OS data structure responsible for state management.

actions.description: Move active thread token from 'New' -> 'Ready' -> 'Running'.
actions.educational_reason: Illustrates OS scheduling dispatch.

actions.description: Transition active thread token from 'Running' to 'Blocked' while writing register state to TCB box.
actions.educational_reason: Visualizes context saving during an I/O wait state.

actions.description: Flash TCB box values updating to reflect saved registers.
actions.educational_reason: Emphasizes CPU register state preservation during context switch.

actions.description: Move token from 'Blocked' -> 'Ready' -> 'Running' -> 'Terminated'.
actions.educational_reason: Completes the lifecycle journey of a thread.

scenes.transition_to_next: Clear lifecycle nodes and set up threading models architecture comparison.

scenes.title: Threading Models: User-Level vs. Kernel-Level
scenes.purpose: Compare how User Threads map to Kernel Threads across Many-to-One, One-to-One, and Many-to-Many models.
scenes.narration: Operating systems map user-level threads to kernel-level execution contexts using different models. The One-to-One model offers high concurrency and multicore usage but higher overhead, while Many-to-One is light but suffers from blocking issues.

relationships.importance: Direct 1:1 mapping between user thread and kernel thread.

actions.description: Establish User Space vs Kernel Space split screen layout.
actions.educational_reason: Delineates privilege boundaries in modern operating systems.

actions.description: Connect UT 1 directly to KT 1, and UT 2 to KT 2.
actions.educational_reason: Demonstrates the 1-to-1 threading model used in Linux and Windows.

actions.description: Change title content to 'Model: Many-to-One (M:1)'.
actions.educational_reason: Prepares transition to single kernel thread mapping.

actions.description: Redirect connection line from UT 2 down to point into KT 1 instead of KT 2, removing KT 2.
actions.educational_reason: Visually transforms architecture into Many-to-One mapping, showing kernel unawareness of individual user threads.

scenes.transition_to_next: Transition into shared memory synchronization and race condition demonstrations.

scenes.title: Race Conditions and Mutex Synchronization
scenes.purpose: Demonstrate visually how uncoordinated shared memory writes corrupt data (race condition) and how a Mutex resolves it.
scenes.narration: When threads access shared data concurrently without synchronization, a race condition occurs. Using a Mutex ensures mutual exclusion so only one thread enters the critical section at a time.

visual_objects.label: Shared Counter
visual_objects.purpose: Shared variable accessible by both threads.

visual_objects.label: Thread B
visual_objects.purpose: Second thread performing concurrent write increment.

visual_objects.label: Mutex Lock
visual_objects.purpose: Synchronization key guarding critical section access.

actions.description: Show counter initialized to 0.
actions.educational_reason: Establishes baseline data value.

actions.description: Thread A reads 0.
actions.educational_reason: Step 1 of un-synchronized write.

actions.description: Thread B reads 0 before Thread A writes back.
actions.educational_reason: Highlights timing overlap leading to race condition.

actions.description: Both threads calculate 0+1=1 and write back 'Value: 1' (Incorrect! Should be 2). Change counter box to RED.
actions.educational_reason: Visually proves data corruption caused by race conditions.

actions.description: Fade in green Mutex Lock icon above counter and reset counter value to 0.
actions.educational_reason: Introduces mutual exclusion solution.

actions.description: Thread A acquires lock: Mutex turns RED ('LOCKED by Thread A'). Thread B is blocked with yellow waiting aura.
actions.educational_reason: Demonstrates exclusive access granted to Thread A while Thread B waits.

actions.description: Thread A updates counter to 1, releases lock. Lock turns back to GREEN. Thread B acquires lock, updates counter to 2.
actions.educational_reason: Proves Mutex ensures correct execution result (Value: 2).

scenes.transition_to_next: Transition from single lock usage into multiple lock deadlock scenario.

scenes.title: Deadlock and Circular Wait
scenes.purpose: Illustrate how improper lock ordering creates an inescapable circular dependency resulting in deadlock.
scenes.narration: Synchronization mechanisms can cause deadlock if threads hold resources while waiting for resources held by each other. This circular wait prevents all involved threads from making progress.

actions.description: Display Thread 1 and Thread 2.
actions.educational_reason: Sets up two concurrent active threads.

actions.description: Show solid line from Thread 1 acquiring Lock A.
actions.educational_reason: Establishes first resource ownership.

actions.description: Show solid line from Thread 2 acquiring Lock B.
actions.educational_reason: Establishes second resource ownership.

actions.description: Draw dashed arrow from Thread 1 requesting Lock B.
actions.educational_reason: Thread 1 blocks waiting for Lock B.

actions.description: Draw dashed arrow from Thread 2 requesting Lock A.
actions.educational_reason: Thread 2 blocks waiting for Lock A, closing the circular dependency loop.

actions.description: Pulse all relationships in bright flashing RED.
actions.educational_reason: Emphasizes frozen execution caused by circular wait condition.

scenes.transition_to_next: Transition to practical thread management architecture using Thread Pools.

scenes.title: Thread Pools & Practical Architecture
scenes.purpose: Demonstrate how thread pools optimize server applications by recycling worker threads rather than destroying and recreating them.
scenes.narration: To avoid creation overhead and resource exhaustion, modern software uses Thread Pools. Incoming tasks enter a queue and are picked up by available reusable worker threads.

visual_objects.label: Incoming Task Queue
visual_objects.purpose: Holds incoming user requests or jobs.

visual_objects.label: Thread Pool
visual_objects.purpose: Container of pre-allocated reusable worker threads.

relationships.importance: Dispatches queued tasks directly onto available idle workers.

actions.description: Show task queue filling with tasks.
actions.educational_reason: Displays request traffic arriving at a system.

actions.description: Display thread pool containing idle workers.
actions.educational_reason: Shows pre-allocated worker threads ready for assignment.

actions.description: Pop 'Task 1' from queue and assign to Worker 1. Worker 1 changes color to GREEN ('Busy').
actions.educational_reason: Illustrates task assignment without overhead of thread creation.

actions.description: Worker 1 completes task and returns to WHITE ('Idle') state ready for next task.
actions.educational_reason: Demonstrates thread reusability.

scenes.transition_to_next: Fade all components into the final integrated architectural view.

final_visual_summary: The final screen displays a unified high-level architecture: A Process container holding shared Memory (Code, Data, Heap), enclosing multiple dynamic Thread paths (with private PC/Registers/Stacks). A small overlay summarizes key dynamics: Concurrency (time slicing) vs Parallelism (multicore), Mutex locks guarding shared state, and Thread Pools managing overall system overhead efficiently.
